html:
The Milograd culture was an Iron Age archaeological culture of southern Belarus and northern Ukraine, around where the Pripyat River joins the Dnieper, from about the 600s BCE to the 1st century CE. It is named after the village of Milahrad in Belarus's Gomel region.

Its people lived in small fortified settlements and open villages near rivers and marshes. They farmed, kept livestock and fished. Their handmade pottery is the main thing that marks the culture out for archaeologists.

Who they were is uncertain. Their language may have been early Baltic or early Slavic, or something in between; the Balto-Slavic languages are thought to have split in roughly this part of Europe. Many scholars identify them with the Neuri, whom Herodotus placed north of the Scythians. He reports a story that every Neurian became a wolf for a few days each year, and that snakes had once driven the Neuri from their land.

Over time the culture came under the influence of newcomers from the northwest linked to the Pomeranian culture, and with them it gave rise to the Zarubintsy culture, which many link to the early Slavs. In the north its lands became part of the Brushed Pottery culture.
